title: Vessantara's giving
hook: the prince who gave past every limit, and the old question about him.
tomorrow: what can you give in a single day that costs no money at all?

segments.voice: A week in six lines. Not the end, even at the quietest place. Food's journey. Four elements. Four protections on one hand. Forty doors. And yesterday, dana: give freely, glad before, bright during, content after.
screen: `NOT THE END.` → `FOOD'S JOURNEY.` → `FOUR ELEMENTS.` → `FOUR PROTECTIONS.` → `FORTY DOORS.` → `GIVE FREELY.`

segments.voice: Most people keep a quiet limit on giving. The old jacket, sure. The car, no. So what would you give away if it cost you nearly everything? Tradition places one prince, Vessantara, in the Buddha's last life before the one in which he woke up, and his story is about giving past every limit. A gentle word for parents: in this story he gives away even his own children, and it's a hard one to hear.
screen: `THE JACKET, SURE. THE CAR, NO.` → `A PRINCE WITH NO LIMIT.` → `A HARD STORY.`

segments.voice: Vessantara is a prince who can't say no to anyone who asks. He gives the kingdom's precious white elephant to envoys from a land in drought, and his own people, furious, send him into exile. On the road out he gives away his chariot and his horses. In the forest, with his wife Maddi and their two children, a greedy old man comes asking for the children as servants, and Vessantara gives them. Then a stranger asks for Maddi. She's given too, and the stranger turns out to be Sakka, king of the gods, who hands her straight back. In the end the children are ransomed by their grandfather, and the family comes home. Here's what's worth noticing. Buddhists didn't pretend this was easy. In the Questions of King Milinda, the king asks the monk Nagasena whether giving away a wife and children was right, and Nagasena has to work to answer. The question sits inside the tradition's own books. What the story teaches, under all that, is today's line: generosity costs. The giving it praises isn't spare change.
screen: `THE WHITE ELEPHANT, THEN EXILE.` · `THE CHILDREN, THEN MADDI.` · `ALL RESTORED IN THE END.` · `KING MILINDA ASKS: WAS IT RIGHT?` · then, large: `GENEROSITY COSTS.`

segments.voice: Hold, or picture, one thing you value that someone else could really use. Notice the pull to keep it, and stay with that pull without obeying it or fighting it. Then ask yourself, quietly: could I give this gladly?
Vessantara's giving: the prince who gave past every limit, in the last of the long Jataka tales. Praised, and argued over.
For the road: generosity costs, and that's part of what makes it generosity. Week done, see you on the other side.

howItsDone: The Vessantara Jataka is retold and performed in Theravada lands, sometimes recited in full at a temple festival; monks and teachers also discuss its hard parts, as the Questions of King Milinda does.
